Ramanujan identified a set of modular equations for eta functions that have been built upon by subsequent mathematicians, including Berndt and Watson, to create more of these identities.  For higher degrees, these can be derived using a specific approach called Hecke collections. This paper provides a comprehensive framework for identifying such collections and uses it to create a set of modular equations for higher degrees than previously explored. Additionally, new collections are discovered that yield additional identities for eta functions.

We have obtained high-resolution near-infrared spectra of eight lensed quasars using the W.M. Keck 1.5-m telescope, utilizing the ESI spectrograph. Our comprehensive analysis, including lens modeling and kinematical analysis, has provided new insights into the redshifts and speed dispersions of the galaxies that are gravitationally lensing quasars. Notably, our results show a significant improvement in precision for the measured redshifts, with a typical uncertainty of 0.0003 and a maximum uncertainty of 0.001. Our findings also reveal a range of speed dispersions, spanning from 300 to 3000 km/s, with a median value of 1400 km/s. These results are consistent with previous studies, although we have identified a discrepancy in the redshift of one of the quasars, SBS1079+245, which we attribute to a misidentification of emission lines in the original study. Our analysis of the lensing galaxies' properties suggests that they are primarily massive early-type galaxies, although we have also identified a few with lower mass and potentially ongoing star formation. Our results also show that the quasars are often offset from the centers of their host galaxies by several kiloparsecs, although we have identified one system in which the quasar is closely aligned with its host galaxy.

This article introduces a novel approach to solving the solvability of nonlinear q-fractional differential equations on a time scale, and derives the existence and uniqueness of solutions for the initial value problems. To this end, we establish a new inequality for the product of functions and derive a key inequality for the product of q-fractional differences. Our findings are supported by a q-fractional variant of the Gronwall-Lemma, and demonstrate that the solutions to these problems exhibit q-harmonically continuous properties.

The emergence of a significant phonon Hall effect in bismuth has been attributed to the topological features of its constant energy surfaces. Our analysis reveals that these surfaces host a Z2 invariant topology characterized by a specific mapping to the 2D torus. By utilizing this mapping, we can derive the topological phonon Berry Hall effect from the fundamental geometric properties of the Z2 invariant constant energy surfaces.

A novel approach to Raman analysis, Shifted Excitation Raman Difference Spectroscopy (SERDS), has been widely adopted for its enhanced sensitivity and speed. This paper presents an optimized method for performing multichannel Raman analysis on various samples, including artistic materials, biological tissues, and microorganisms. The proposed technique achieves high signal-to-noise ratios of up to 100 times greater than conventional methods, allowing for detailed spectral analysis of broad field samples. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through successful Raman imaging of artworks, microbial colonies, and tumor cells.

This study focuses on matrix analogs of Fej\'{e}r and Levin-Ste\v{c}kin inequalities. Specifically, it derives matrix versions of these inequalities for interpolative and subordinating inequalities within the context of Fej\'{e}r and Levin-Ste\v{c}kin type matrices, respectively.

We examine the mean null energy condition for the event horizon of a four-dimensional Schwarzschild black hole undergoing evaporation. We find that the condition is violated at early stages, but subsequently becomes valid as the black hole approaches evaporation. Notably, the mean null energy condition is broken initially due to the presence of a negative energy flux through the horizon, but it is restored once the self-gravity of the horizon on long timescales becomes significant.

This lecture note serves as a comprehensive overview of the basic principles of Conformal Field Theory (CFT), commencing with an in-depth exploration of the conformal group and its applications, including the calculation of key three and four-point functions. Subsequent sections cover the introduction of operators that possess conformal properties, followed by a detailed examination of the primary fields and their actions within both Euclidean and Minkowskian spacetime scenarios. The notes also touch upon key aspects of the duality between Euclidean and Minkowskian CFTs in two dimensions, the Kac-Moody algebra, the KZ equations, and an introduction to Liouville and Toda field theories.

This research presents the ICS-CTM2, a cybersecurity evaluation framework model for industrial control systems that addresses the complexities of real-world cybersecurity challenges faced by ICS vendors. The ICS-CTM2 is a refinement of the widely used Software Engineering Body of Knowledge (SEBOK) Control and Technical Metrics model, adapted to meet the specific needs of the industrial control systems' software development. The ICS-CTM2 model is a key component of a comprehensive cybersecurity evaluation framework for ICS, as well as a crucial element of a proposed cybersecurity metrics standard for ICS, announced in a separate publication.

In multi-agent reinforcement learning, the challenge of coordinating multiple agents in complex, dynamic environments is a significant concern. The value function, which assesses the cumulative reward, is a key concept in this field, but its effectiveness is limited when rewards are small and varied in size. To address this issue, we introduce a new value function approach, called the avaricious value function, which takes into account individual agent preferences to assign greater importance to collective rewards. Through simulations of traffic light control tasks, we have found that our proposed method outperforms traditional value function approaches, demonstrating its potential to enhance ideal coordination in multi-agent reinforcement learning scenarios.

Recent studies have shown that widely used language models exhibit prejudice-based biases. Our investigation focuses on stereotypical traits like age, race, sex, and sexual orientation and their impact on these models. We introduce StereoSet, a new evaluation tool that assesses prejudice-based biases in stereo profiles, comprising brief profiles featuring individuals of various stereo characteristics. This dataset is used to evaluate 9 models, including 6 large language models and 3 smaller models, across 4 tasks, demonstrating that large language models exhibit more prejudice-based biases than smaller models, with a notable exception in the case of racial bias in sexual orientation.

The widespread adoption of renewable energy in modern power grids necessitates innovative methods for optimizing power generation. This research focuses on optimizing the tilt of solar panels in solar-powered electrical vehicles, a critical factor that affects power output and battery efficiency. Our study demonstrates that the tilt angles of solar panels in solar-powered EVs exhibit a predictable pattern in response to changes in state of charge, enabling the use of predictive models to forecast panel orientation. This approach offers several advantages, including reduced energy losses and enhanced battery life, improved energy output predictability, and increased model transparency. Our experiments with real-world data validate the effectiveness of this method, showcasing improved power generation, enhanced predictability, and increased transparency compared to a control strategy.

This paper delves into the geometric properties of a specific type of ellipsoid, where the ratio of its semi-axes is expressed through a formula involving the cosine of a given angle, yielding a result that's not as straightforward as one might expect. By employing an approach that's distinct from, yet related to, the traditional method of coordinate transformation, we explore the complex symmetries of this particular ellipsoid. Ultimately, our analysis leads to a notable observation regarding the interplay between geometric complexity and symmetry, where the intricate nature of an object does not necessarily equate to a lack of symmetry.

The expansion of personal data markets, driven by the growth of data-driven platforms, has been fueled by research aimed at understanding their potential impact. While previous studies have primarily focused on how data markets can benefit these platforms, our investigation explores the other side of the equation and examines how individuals respond to the creation and trade of personal data markets. Our research, conducted on a platform that enables users to sell their online activity data, offers a unique opportunity to study how individuals interact with data markets. Our findings reveal that users are cautious when sharing their personal data, even when given the option to do so. Conversely, we also found that users are willing to participate in data markets, especially when monetary incentives are involved, as we observed users selling their data for low sums. However, our study also highlights the importance of data market design, as some users may engage in strategic data selling practices, such as partitioning, to maximize their gains.

In the context of deep learning, a novel approach is proposed for identifying FTN constellations through list S-decoding. To address this challenge, a modified S-decoding technique is developed, which involves constructing a list of spheres around candidate solutions. To optimize this method, a neural network is trained to generate candidate solutions based on the received signal. The proposed technique is evaluated for QPSK-modulated FTN signals with varying sampling rates and for different channel conditions, demonstrating its ability to achieve a 3 dB improvement in signal-to-noise ratio over traditional methods.

Impact algebras were introduced by Harbin Reiter and are a variation of De Morgan algebras used to model decision-making scenarios. These algebras have been found to be either totally ordered or semilattice-ordered. The order of impact algebras has been found to be consistent with their topological structure. This paper aims to explore the properties of these algebras when ordered in a particular way and their topological structure. It also investigates and classifies the possible forms of ideals in these algebras and their topological structure.

A key technique for enhancing deep neural network generalization is data augmentation, which can be enhanced by saliency maps to focus on the most informative image areas. By leveraging these maps, the model learns more effectively from relevant features, thereby improving its generalization capabilities. Our proposed method, SaliencyMix, integrates saliency maps to create a more effective data augmentation technique. In each iteration, the method randomly replaces image segments with equivalent patches from a random set, thereby introducing greater variability. Experimental evaluations on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet datasets demonstrate that SaliencyMix outperforms conventional data augmentation methods, yielding improved performance in both training speed and model accuracy.

We investigate certain infinite-dimensional Lie algebras $\mathfrak{g}$ and their associated Iwahori--Hecke algebras $\mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{g})$, with specific methods applied to trace-symmetric elements. A particular method, involving an extension of the Gelfand--Graev representation, is employed to construct a $\mathcal{W}$-module with a $\mathcal{H}$-action, derived from a $\mathcal{W}$-module with a $\mathfrak{g}$-action. Additionally, an infinite-dimensional generalization of a $\mathcal{W}$-module with a $\mathfrak{g}$-action is constructed, based on a $\mathfrak{g}$-module with a $\mathfrak{g}$-action.

A new method is proposed that combines two approaches to measure the alignment of galaxy orientations with their surroundings, using data from the Euclid survey. This method provides a way to test alternative gravity theories, particularly those that alter the way space and matter interact in the universe. The proposed method involves analyzing how galaxies are affected by the gravitational potential around them, as well as the way in which light is distorted as it travels through the universe's gravitational fields. This analysis can be used to compare different gravity theories, including those that are slightly altered from the standard model. The proposed method is shown to be effective in constraining the way in which gravity is modified in the universe, particularly in the case of a particular type of gravity theory known as Horndeski.

In the field of soft condensed matter, the study of pliable particles has garnered significant attention. By examining the dynamic properties of these particles through numerical simulations, we have discovered unique rheological behaviors in systems with pliable particles. Notably, the solid-like response to shear stress exhibits a distinct solidification threshold below which the system behaves like a fluid. This solidification threshold is characterized by a non-zero shear rate, unlike the traditional solidification of amorphous materials, which occurs at a zero shear rate. This non-zero threshold is a result of the particles' ability to slide past one another, giving rise to a shear stress even when the shear rate is zero. Furthermore, the system's behavior is influenced by the range of interactions between particles, which can lead to a transition from a solid-like response to a fluid-like one. This transition is marked by a non-zero shear rate, below which the system exhibits solid-like properties. Interestingly, the system's behavior is also sensitive to the level of stiffness in the particles, which can cause a transition from a solid-like response to a fluid-like one. This research has significant implications for the study of soft materials, which are increasingly important in various applications, including those found in the human body.

A novel computational approach is proposed that seamlessly integrates empirical potential models with first-principles simulations. This methodology enables the creation of a potential function that accurately represents the behavior of gold nanoparticles across various temperatures and particle sizes. Through a series of molecular dynamics simulations, the potential is validated by accurately predicting the structural changes in gold nanoparticles as temperature increases, including the melting of smaller particles. Furthermore, this simulation framework is utilized to establish a statistical model that quantitatively describes the melting behavior of gold nanoparticles, taking into account both thermodynamic and size-specific factors. This model is then applied to predict the melting behavior of larger gold particles, and the results are found to be consistent with experimental observations.

In this study, we have developed a parameterized division theorem for a specific class of operators known as potential operators, which operate within a particular Banach space. The class of potential operators encompasses a broad range of significant functionals, including those used in the analysis of partial differential equations, dynamical systems, and functional analysis. Our research builds upon a previous division theorem for bounded operators, but the operators in question here are not necessarily bounded. Instead, they are characterized by a particular growth property, which is crucial to deriving a division theorem. The growth property is a key aspect of our theory and has significant implications for the operators' behavior. Furthermore, our theory is closely tied to the concept of bifurcations, which occur when a parameter in an operator changes, leading to a new operator with distinct properties. The growth property plays a pivotal role in understanding these bifurcations and their structure.

The concept of taste is often seen as a complex system with multiple flavors, but this perception is misleading. Research suggests that taste experiences can be categorized into four primary categories: sweet, bitter, sour, and savory. This framework is rooted in the structure of taste receptors found on the tongue, which are responsible for detecting specific molecules responsible for different tastes. Interestingly, this four-part model is also reflected in the patterns of neural connections in the brain, which are linked to the same molecules responsible for taste receptors. This study proposes a new model, which reduces the complexity of taste by mapping it onto a tetrahedron, and argues that there is a fundamental relationship between the taste experience and the molecules responsible for it. This model also suggests that individual differences in taste preferences are not due to the presence of new taste types, but rather the result of unique variations in the perception of these molecules.

This paper establishes identities for the (h; q)-Genocchi numbers and polynomials, invents two new (h; q)-numbers, and creates novel representations for the Frobenius--Chudnovsky--Euler polynomials, Riemann zeta function, and Gamma function, in addition to generalizing the Williams--Watson identity for the (h; q)-Genocchi polynomials.

This research introduces a novel machine learning technique to determine the long-term impact of treatment on patient outcomes. By analyzing the long-term effects of treatment on patient health, this method enables early identification of those who can benefit most from specific treatments. Building on the latest developments in reinforcement learning, this technique leverages long-term rewards to make predictions. To enhance model interpretability, we incorporate a feature selection module, allowing clinicians to pinpoint key factors driving long-term treatment effects. Through experiments using synthetic and real-world data, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our model in predicting long-term treatment effects, while also providing actionable insights into underlying factors.

Retrospective case-control studies are frequently used in epidemiology to investigate the correlation between past exposure and current health outcomes. However, participants' recollections of their past exposures are often influenced by their current health status, leading to the use of case-control studies. While numerous methods have been developed to address this issue, they typically rely on the assumption that recall distortions do not depend on unobserved factors. However, this assumption is frequently violated, resulting in biased estimates of causal effects. This study proposes a causal inference framework that accounts for recall distortions dependent on unobserved factors. We develop a method to estimate the causal effects of exposure on disease incidence using data from case-control studies, and demonstrate its application in a simulation study and a real-world study examining the relationship between exposure to pesticides and Parkinson's disease.

Generative autoencoders, which are trained using reconstruction loss, can be used to identify the most informative data features. However, their reconstruction loss can be challenging to maximize to the full extent. We have developed a novel approach to train generative autoencoders, which involves utilizing utmost likelihood training to achieve the full potential of the model. By applying this method to a real-world dataset, we found that it can effectively identify the most critical features of the data. Our solution uses a unique combination of standard machine learning techniques and invertible layers, which allows for the efficient and precise training of generative models. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of our method by applying it to a real-world dataset, which resulted in a more accurate and efficient data representation.

Cities are rapidly evolving, driven by technological advancements, demographic shifts, and economic growth. As a result, they are facing a multitude of complex issues, from natural disasters to social problems, which can be attributed to their urban structures and processes. The increasing availability of data from various sources, including sensors, social media, and administrative records, presents an opportunity to gain insights into city dynamics. Nevertheless, the sheer volume and diversity of this data, combined with its inherent complexity, pose significant challenges to understanding urban phenomena. To address this, we propose an innovative approach that leverages machine learning and visualization techniques to facilitate the analysis of urban data. Our method enables users to identify key features and their interconnections, which can then be utilized to extract meaningful patterns. The analysis of these patterns allows us to uncover underlying structures and processes that are not immediately apparent. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to a real-world urban data set, and we provide a user guide that outlines the necessary steps and considerations for successful implementation.

This study explores the numerical solution of two-dimensional reaction-diffusion equations and generalized Stokes systems using the HDG-P0 method, which is implemented with a low-order polynomial space for approximation. To enhance convergence rates in iterative schemes, we introduce an optimal geometric multigrid preconditioner that can be effectively integrated into HDG-P0 methods. To this end, we establish a theoretical framework to prove the optimal convergence rate of the multigrid method, which is then applied to reaction-diffusion equations and generalized Stokes systems. Numerical experiments are conducted to validate the proposed approach.

The prevalence of missing data in studies makes it crucial to consider the impact of these data gaps on the reliability of findings. While multiple approaches have been developed to address this issue, there remains a need for a more rigorous sensitivity analysis that provides evidence-based conclusions. This research introduces a Bayesian sensitivity analysis method that leverages the E-value framework to quantify the reliability of findings in the face of missing data. By comparing the results of this approach to a traditional maximum likelihood method, we demonstrate its effectiveness in examining the evidence for the association between a binary outcome and two covariates in a study with 20% missing data. The analysis reveals that the Bayesian method yields more conservative and precise results than the maximum likelihood method, and its output is less influenced by the choice of prior distribution.

A recent study by Kieska and Kim (2021) proposed a Bayesian framework for assessing missing information in multivariate trials with various types of dropouts. However, this approach has a limitation in being applicable only to normal data and a further issue with its interpretation. In contrast, we suggest an alternative method grounded in the probability of observing missing data, allowing for the evaluation of missing information without relying on specific distributional assumptions. Furthermore, we examine the properties of this probability-based approach and provide a case study to illustrate its application.

A category can be considered feeble monoidal if its product and equalizer functors can be composed to form a functor that aligns with its unit, under a specific arrangement. In such cases, we demonstrate the existence of a stochastic operator that maps a category to a simplicial complex, by representing the coalgebra associated with a monoidal category as a specific type of simplicial complex, known as a Stasheff A∞-coalgebra, referred to as a feeble category. This concept is further explored through examples of a monoidal category formed from a group and a category of sets, as well as a more general scenario involving a category of a specific structure.

In DRAM, the memory cell is triggered to release its charge by applying a specific voltage. The amount of time taken for the DRAM to complete this process is known as the refresh time, which is typically determined by the DRAM manufacturer. The traditional method of refreshing DRAM involves periodically applying a refresh cycle to ensure that the data remains valid even after the RAS timing limit is exceeded. However, the implementation of the refresh policy is solely based on the DRAM manufacturer's expertise and does not allow for any customization.

In this research, the Codic framework is introduced to allow for the customization of the DRAM refresh policy. Codic is a DRAM substrate that enables the modification of the DRAM's refresh time. This paper is the second installment in a series exploring the role of functional programming in designing and managing virtualized networks. It delves into the concept of network evolution, where an existing network is modified or upgraded, and explains the importance of a structured approach to ensure seamless system changes. By applying design principles, one can effectively plan and implement these upgrades, thereby avoiding potential disruptions to the network.

To investigate the role of multi-qubit operations in quantum error correction, we analyze the toric code within a lattice model. We compare the performance of two-qubit and multi-qubit operations in stabilizer-based protocols, specifically examining the toric code's behavior in a noisy environment with a variable probability of bit-flip errors. The results show that while two-qubit operations are essential for encoding and decoding, multi-qubit measurements can be used to measure the energy of excited states, enabling a more energy-efficient approach to measurement. We demonstrate that this approach can be used to estimate the accuracy of the toric code's decoder, allowing for a more energy-efficient assessment of its performance.

The OPUS system is a universal job management system that supports multiple protocols, including those defined by the VO standards, as well as by the Globus GridFTP and X.509 authentication/PTI-based GridFTP standards. It is designed to handle a wide range of file transfer tasks efficiently and effectively, even in the event of system failures. OPUS is currently being utilized in various production environments, including large-scale scientific projects like ALMA and the Chilean National ALMA factory, as well as the Brazilian Southern Observatory.

Teaching complex, interactive topics such as Wireless Ad Hoc networks in computer science education poses significant challenges, including limited student engagement and understanding. To address these issues, this paper proposes an innovative approach that integrates interactive learning through digital game-enhanced learning. This approach leverages real-world simulations of wireless networks and incorporates game elements to make the learning experience more immersive and effective. To evaluate its impact, a pilot study was conducted with undergraduate students, who were divided into two groups: those who participated in the game-enhanced learning experience and those who followed a traditional teaching method. The results of the study revealed that students who engaged with the game-enhanced learning experience demonstrated significantly higher levels of knowledge acquisition compared to their peers.

The relationship between molecular oxygen and ozone has been used as a key indicator for detecting biosignatures in exoplanetary systems, but this approach may not be reliable due to ozone's dual roles in atmospheric chemistry. To assess its effectiveness, a study was conducted using high-fidelity simulations of Earth-like atmospheres, which showed that ozone levels are not consistently correlated with oxygen levels across various scenarios. The study found that ozone production and destruction are influenced by different factors, leading to a more complex and uncertain relationship between ozone and oxygen. As a result, relying solely on ozone as a biosignature proxy may not be advisable, and alternative methods for characterizing habitability should be explored.

We investigate the Hofstadter model in three dimensions, which exhibits a variety of quantum states influenced by the magnetic field strength, resulting in diverse quantum Hall states. Our study reveals that the quantum Hall states of two-dimensional systems can be stabilized in three-dimensional space by confining particles within a specific area using harmonic potentials. This leads to the emergence of non-equilibrium surface currents driven by the Peierls mechanism, which can be manipulated using adjustable gates. Our findings suggest that the Hofstadter model in three dimensions provides a feasible experimental platform for simulating non-equilibrium quantum states of two-dimensional systems.

Recent advancements in multilingual neural machine translation (NMT) have made it possible to translate text across multiple languages with a single model. However, the effectiveness of this approach is still being explored, particularly when applied to specialized domains. This study investigates how multilingual NMT pre-trained on domains from the medical field performs in various translation tasks. We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of 12 different tasks, comparing the performance of multilingual models to that of monolingual models. The results show that multilingual models pre-trained on domains from the medical field outperform monolingual models in medical translation tasks, with a significant improvement of 8.2 BLEU points.

A theoretical study of the nonlinear interaction between a nonthermal electron population and a population of positively charged background ions within a plasma is conducted. The investigation focuses on how the properties of the positively charged background ions, specifically their temperature and density, influence the creation of solitary and shock waves in a two-dimensional framework. The study reveals the emergence of distinct types of solitary and shock waves, which are dependent on background ion temperature and nonthermal electron density. The results demonstrate that the presence of background ions can significantly reduce the amplitude of solitary waves, while their density and temperature also play a crucial role in shaping the waveforms. Furthermore, it is found that the amplitude of shock waves is highly dependent on background ion temperature and nonthermal electron density. The study also examines the effects of positively charged background ions on wave propagation and reveals that the waveforms can be either compressed or expanded, depending on background ion density. The results also show that the presence of positively charged background ions can significantly reduce the background electron density, which is in agreement with experimental observations.

Recent breakthroughs in research have shown that pretraining language models on sentence embeddings can significantly boost the performance of information retrieval systems. However, the current approaches are mainly confined to English and other widely spoken languages, while the development of multilingual sentence embedding models for information retrieval has received relatively less attention. This study aims to bridge this gap by proposing a novel pretraining method that utilizes an unsupervised context-aware sentence embedding approach, which is then applied to a diverse set of languages, including English, French, German, Japanese, and others. The results of our experiments conducted on a multilingual dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, outperforming the existing state-of-the-art models in various dense retrieval tasks.

Multimodal representation learning, a significant area of research in education, has been hindered by the lack of comprehensive, annotated datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel dataset called EdMoED, which encompasses a wide range of education-related tasks, such as predicting student performance and academic skills. EdMoED is a unique, multimodal dataset that combines real-world data from online education platforms and in-depth teacher evaluations. To effectively utilize this dataset, we propose a new method, Prototypical Mode Rebalance (PMR), which leverages a contrastive learning approach to improve the accuracy of multimodal representations. By using PMR to pre-train a model on EdMoED, we achieve state-of-the-art results across various education-related tasks, outperforming existing methods by a significant margin. The proposed approach is particularly effective in handling noisy data and is scalable for real-world applications.

This research paper presents a theoretical framework for the movement of suspended particles in a vertical, vertically oscillating system. The study focuses on the behavior of these particles within a narrow range of frequencies, specifically the resonance frequency, where the particles' movement is significantly amplified. A mathematical equation describing the movement of these particles at resonance has been developed, and it includes variables representing the frequency and amplitude of the oscillations as well as the characteristics of the fluid and the particles. The new equation expands upon an existing theory by incorporating vector parameters that account for the particles' orientation and engagement with the fluid, which the study's authors argue is a crucial factor in the movement of these particles at resonance. The study's equations were verified through numerical simulations and a comparison with experimental data. The study's conclusions were also validated by analyzing data from a previous experiment. The study's authors also provide a mathematical representation of the movement of these particles at resonance in the form of a vector field.

This study presents a novel end-to-end deep learning model for spoken command recognition, specifically designed to handle the complex audio signals from robotic arms, which are commonly used in the field. To overcome the limitations of traditional CNN-LSTM models when processing such signals, we introduce a Tensor-Trainer Network (TTN) that employs a novel block structure and benefits from low-rank tensor properties. Furthermore, we propose a hybrid TTN model that combines TTNs with other neural network architectures to achieve superior performance. Experimental results on the TACO dataset demonstrate the efficacy of our method, which surpasses the performance of CNN-LSTM models by 10% in the word error rate metric. Additionally, our approach exhibits enhanced interpretability and adaptability to handle long and noisy robotic arm audio signals.

The behavior of a two-level system interacting with a quantum oscillator can be described by two distinct master equations, one based on the Schrödinger and the other on the Dirac representation of the system's wave function. A key aspect of this system is the existence of quantum-jump pathways that facilitate the system's evolution. Notably, the quantum-jump pathways based on the Dirac representation exhibit distinct features compared to those derived from the Schrödinger representation, making it a valuable reference for experimental investigations.

Theoretical analysis was conducted to investigate the effect of varying the ratio of aluminum nano-particle form on the absorption spectrum of thin-film silicon solar cells. Two different aluminum nano-particle forms were considered: spherical and almond-shaped. A 2D model was employed to simulate the absorption spectra of the solar cells, and the results showed that the almond-shaped nanoparticles exhibited higher absorption across a broader wavelength range compared to spherical nanoparticles. Moreover, increasing the concentration of aluminum nano-particles led to enhanced absorption in both cases.

In descriptive complexity theory, non-hereditary properties are a focus, particularly those that can be expressed using first-order logic and additional language elements such as enumeration and set operations. Researchers have been exploring the boundaries of computational complexity by analyzing the impact of these elements, particularly the set operations that can be applied to them. Initially, this investigation centered on the class PTIME, with some surprising outcomes, including the demonstration that even without certain advanced tools, PTIME can still be expressed using first-order logic and additional language elements. Conversely, another key class, NP, has been shown to be beyond the reach of these tools, even if they are applied in a certain manner. This research has also led to the development of a new tool, the selection operator, which has been found to be a key factor in expressing PTIME but not NP.

Deep learning has revolutionized video analysis by enabling the extraction of complex features from large datasets through deep neural networks. However, the high power consumption of these models hinders their real-world application, particularly in IoT devices with limited resources. To address this challenge, we present an efficient implementation of deep learning models for video analysis, focusing on the reduction of power consumption through a combination of software and hardware optimizations. To achieve this, we first develop an energy-efficient software solution by reconfiguring the model's architecture using tensor decomposition, which significantly reduces computational complexity without compromising accuracy. We then integrate this software solution into a hardware accelerator, which is a field-programmable gate array (FPGA). The resulting hardware is a tensor core processor that leverages hierarchical Tucker decomposition to efficiently perform matrix multiplication and outperforms traditional FPGA-based deep neural networks in terms of power efficiency and performance.

The MAVLink protocol, used by the ArduPilot and PX4 projects, is a widely adopted standard for communication in the unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) industry. However, its security has not been thoroughly investigated until now. This paper presents MAVSec, a security framework designed to safeguard the MAVLink protocol against potential threats. MAVSec's security features include a robust authentication mechanism, which prevents unauthorized access to MAVLink connections, as well as a comprehensive encryption method to protect the communication between the MAVLink protocol and the device. Additionally, MAVSec introduces a secure channel protocol, which ensures the integrity and confidentiality of UAV commands and system data. MAVSec's effectiveness has been successfully demonstrated through a series of rigorous testing, which simulates real-world UAV system attacks. The results of the security evaluation indicate that MAVSec's security features provide a strong level of protection against malicious UAV system attacks.

Kollaps is a distributed, flexible simulation tool designed to mimic the
structure and behavior of complex systems over time. Its scalable design and
ability to adapt both its structure and timing make it suitable for modeling
systems that grow, change, evolve, or adapt rapidly. Kollaps's modular design
permits users to model various system types, from simple linear processes to
complex networks with multiple nodes, and from static systems to highly
dynamic environments. Through a series of examples, we demonstrate Kollaps's
capacity to model diverse system configurations and behaviors. We assess the
performance of Kollaps in terms of its computational efficiency and scalability.
Our experiments reveal that Kollaps effectively emulates large, intricate
systems, even when run on a single processor, and that its performance is
insensitive to the number of nodes it is split across.
The Newman-Penrose map's origins in twistor space are explored in relation to its starting point.

The detection of cosmic rays by muons offers a valuable tool for creating detailed underground maps, particularly in geoscience applications, where researchers can infer the density of subterranean regions by measuring the rate at which muons pass through. This phenomenon can be accurately measured using scintillators, yet these detectors have limitations in capturing the full range of muon energies. In contrast, muon telescopes that utilize the full muon energy spectrum can provide a more precise measurement of the density of subterranean regions, thus enabling researchers to create detailed underground maps. This study outlines the design, simulation, and analysis of a compact, all-silicon muon telescope designed for underground density mapping.

A parsing expression grammar (PEG) is a parsing approach that uses a PEG to define a left-recursive grammar, which can cause a PEG parser to enter an infinite loop. GLLL is a technique that prevents a PEG parser from entering this loop by reordering the PEG to avoid left recursion, replacing it with right recursive grammars, which can then be parsed using a bottom-up parser like LL(1). In this paper, a PEG LLr parser was implemented and tested on a range of languages, including HTML, CSS, Java, and C# code, by first converting these left-recursive grammars to right-recursive grammars, which the GLLL algorithm then optimized for LL(1) parsing. The parser was also used to parse the HTML, CSS, Java, and C# languages, which were then analyzed for syntax errors.

In the presence of a parallel electric and magnetic field, we have examined the phenomenon of vacuum Cherenkov radiation at temperatures non-zero, using a specific field theoretical model. This study has led to the conclusion that thermal effects can significantly enhance the rate of radiation. A notable aspect of our findings is the existence of a threshold photon mass at absolute zero, which is a characteristic feature. However, at non-zero temperatures, this threshold is no longer present and the rate of radiation is found to be higher than that at absolute zero temperature.

Language prediction is a complex issue that has been extensively studied in both cognitive sciences and computational linguistics.  While cognitive theories provide insight into the rules governing language, computational models such as neural networks offer a more accurate representation of language patterns.  However, the relationship between cognitive and computational models remains poorly understood.  In this study, we investigate the connection between human language forecasting abilities and the performance of artificial neural networks, trained on massive amounts of text data.  We also examine how language forecasting tasks influence the way people anticipate upcoming words and how these tasks modify the structure of words, using a naturalistic approach.  Our findings indicate that artificial neural networks, trained on large amounts of text data, are capable of accurately predicting words in both short and long-term contexts, and that the memory span of these models is similar to that of humans.  Our research also reveals that humans and artificial neural networks share similar strategies for language forecasting, and that the way people anticipate upcoming words is influenced by cognitive factors and task type.

In this research, we explore a novel approach to determining three-dimensional object positioning by analyzing object rotation. We demonstrate that observing an object's rotation can provide insight into its three-dimensional structure, and that this knowledge can be leveraged to estimate the object's positioning in a scene. To achieve this, we introduce a method for extracting motion trajectories from the object's rotation, and utilize a deep learning model to interpret these trajectories and estimate the object's three-dimensional structure. Notably, our proposed method excels in situations where direct visual observations are limited or impermissible, and it can also be applied to scenarios with partial or incomplete three-dimensional structure.

We investigate the influence of an applied gate voltage on Andreev bound states within a hybrid structure consisting of an SNS junction in a quantum dot, with a single channel for transport. Our calculations demonstrate that the zero-energy AB states can be manipulated through the S layer's potential, allowing for control over crossed Andreev reflection and elastic co-tunneling. Our results reveal that the ratio of these processes changes significantly with the S layer's potential, with a notable shift from CAVR dominance at negative potentials to ECT dominance at positive potentials. Our findings show that the CAVR process can be fully suppressed, while the S layer can be used to control the ECT process, with a notable increase of up to 100% with an applied potential.

A novel method, called the 'angle-of-attack scattering' (AAS) model, has been developed to explain the 'particle boosting' phenomenon commonly observed in magnetic reconnection. This new model incorporates a scattering mechanism that depends on the angle of incidence, in addition to the existing magnetic drift mechanism, to account for the observed particle acceleration. The inclusion of AAS significantly enhances the efficiency of particle acceleration, particularly in low-drift-exhibition configurations. Furthermore, the AAS model provides a more accurate description of the velocity distribution function in magnetic reconnection, as evidenced by its improved agreement with the observed results.

In the Standard Model, a new, heavy, and neutral scalar particle, $Z_h$, is introduced via the Standard Model's $Z$ and Higgs bosons. This particle is generated through the process $e^+e^- \to Z h$, which is a prime target for future linear colliders. This study explores the potential of a 3 TeV linear collider to detect the $e^+e^- \to Z h$ signal in the presence of additional heavy scalars. It also examines the effect of these scalars on the Higgs diphoton decay rate.

This paper examines the subdifferential of the collective numerical range, defined by the convex hull of the spectral norms of all unitary transformations of a specific matrix in complex linear algebra. We establish that the subdifferential of the collective numerical range exists for normal matrices and can be represented as a combination of the spectral norms of corresponding adjoint transformations. Furthermore, we derive an alternative expression for this subdifferential when the input matrices are unitary.

The growing adoption of cloud computing has led to increasing concerns over user privacy.  Differential privacy provides a theoretical guarantee for confidential data, but its practical implementation is hindered by significant noise addition required to achieve sufficient privacy.  This noise significantly degrades the utility of the output, prompting the exploration of more efficient mechanisms.  Our research focuses on developing a more effective mechanism that utilizes a unique payment system, allowing users to offset the costs associated with noise addition through improved utility.  Our analysis reveals that the most efficient mechanisms are those that utilize the greatest amount of noise, leading us to propose a new payment system that prioritizes noise addition at the expense of payment.  Additionally, we examine the implications of user behavior in the context of monetary privacy and introduce a novel mechanism that utilizes user feedback to inform the optimal noise level.

A novel stochastic approach to assigning variables is presented, which involves a random vector taking values in a given manifold and being represented as a local coordinate system. This vector is subject to certain constraints and follows a specific probability distribution, defined by a positive function on the manifold. The proposed framework is applied to the space of discrete allocations, where it is shown that the function can be interpreted as a correlation measure. The resulting theory is utilized to establish a set of axioms for a local function on the allocation space, which can be realized as a function on a manifold. The proposed approach is demonstrated through various examples, including discrete allocations, permutation groups, and the space of all possible graphs.

The development of laser-driven compression experiments to study inertial confinement and the synthesis of new materials relies on accurately predicting the behavior of gases under intense laser compression. To this end, researchers have investigated how high-energy lasers initiate combustion in dense helium and hydrogen mixtures at pressures of up to 500 times the atmospheric pressure. To study this process, they used a technique called laser photodetionization, which involved exposing the gas to a high-energy laser to break down its molecular state and create a plasma. The resulting plasma was then analyzed using a technique called time-of-flight mass spectrometry, which revealed the formation of hydrogen and other species within a few nanoseconds of exposure. The researchers found that the amount of hydrogen and other species produced increased with higher laser intensities, but also found that the gas reached a point of equilibrium where more energy input did not produce more reactive species. The researchers were able to study the gas's behavior at various conditions, including its ability to ignite at different temperatures and the amount of energy required to reach a certain state. The results of this study are expected to contribute to a better understanding of gas behavior under intense laser compression.

A new, compact network for segmenting images has been developed, which can efficiently process images on low-power devices in real-time. The network, which is called CompResNet, uses a combination of convolutional and pooling layers to segment images and a single layer to identify the objects in each segment. The compact design of the network allows it to run quickly on mobile devices, even with limited processing power. The accuracy of the CompResNet network has been tested on images of objects in various environments and compares favorably with other leading image segmentation techniques.

Automated vehicles are now equipped with communication technology that enables them to exchange information with other vehicles and infrastructure. However, this communication method has limitations in sharing data with non-vehicle road users, such as pedestrians. To address this, a new study proposes a driver messenger network that allows drivers to share messages with each other. The study's findings are based on a driver survey and reveal that drivers are willing to share information with each other if it is relevant and useful, particularly for safety purposes. The study also suggests that driver messenger networks can be used to facilitate lane changes and suggests several design principles for such applications.

The behavior of passive particles in the presence of a moving boundary can be studied using a mathematical model, specifically the advection-diffusion equation, to understand how particles are transported in various spatial environments. We investigate the transport of non-interacting particles in different geometries, including infinite, circular, and confined environments, with specific boundary conditions, and derive the effective diffusion coefficient using a novel approach based on time-averaged currents. We also compare the transport behavior in these environments with a theoretical prediction based on the stationary probability distribution and discuss the impact of different boundary conditions on particle movement.

For a highly excited two-dimensional atom in a uniform magnetic field, interacting with a two-dimensional, two-component electromagnetic wave, the wave function is approximated by a Gaussian distribution with a small, adjustable correction. A set of nonlinear differential equations describing the evolution of this distribution and its correction are derived, and the boundary conditions are determined. By solving these equations subject to Siegert conditions, the corrected Gaussian wave function is expressed in terms of error functions. The behavior of this distribution is analyzed for long and short times, and for intermediate times, especially near the resonance frequency. The results are compared with the behavior of a Dicke model, and the effects of the correction on the atom's dynamics are explored.

Observations made by the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS) have revealed rapid changes in Si IV line emission fluctuations during a solar flare. These fluctuations occurred at a sub-second rate and were accompanied by changes in coronal hard X-rays and EUV emission. High-resolution observations show that the Si IV line emission changes occurred in two distinct regions, each spanning approximately 3 arcseconds. Analysis of these changes suggests that they result from the suppression and enhancement of downflowing plasma. Furthermore, the sub-second variations in Si IV line intensity are found to be highly correlated with plasma dynamics, specifically with the speed and direction of the plasma currents.

In the context of the strong CP problem, a new type of Peccei-Quinn symmetry is introduced, which is distinct from the original U(1) PQ symmetry, but instead forms an additional, non-standard D-term in the Lagrangian. This new term leads to a mass for the pseudo-scalar particle, which is a solution to the strong CP problem, that differs from the axion. Specifically, the mass of the pseudo-scalar is determined by the Planck scale and the mass of the quark, which is within the range of experimental measurement. This new type of PQ symmetry also affects the behavior of a specific electric dipole moment, which is a measure of certain particle properties, leading to a prediction that this particular electric dipole moment will eventually reach a stable point.

Theoretical analysis of self-annealing in thin layers is conducted under the assumption that thermal energy is not sufficient to impede atomic motion.  The study focuses on the impact of nonthermal processes on the movement of atoms, specifically the role of local atomic rearrangement energies and the physical properties of the material.  The concept of collision cascades is used to determine the energy required for displacement, denoted as $T_{d}$.  The displaced atoms are assumed to be distributed uniformly throughout a sphere with a radius equal to $T_{d}$.  The displaced atoms are then subject to thermal diffusion, with the effective diffusion length determined by the radius of the collision cascade.  The distribution of displaced atoms is calculated using a modified version of the standard Fickian self-diffusion equation.  The theoretical model is validated by comparing its results to experimental measurements of the critical angle for various materials, including GaS, InS, and GaAs.  The study finds that the model accurately predicts the critical angle for these materials, provided that the model parameters are adjusted to account for the unique physical properties of each material.

This study presents a method to hinder the practicality of code plagiarism detection by obscuring source code structure, thereby disrupting traditional control-flow and data-flow analysis techniques. The navigation approach is employed to identify key concepts in source code, thereby disrupting standard analysis methods. The efficacy of this approach is evaluated by implementing a modified call graph analysis in a C# environment.

Consider the series $F(s) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n e^{lb_n(s)}$, where $a_n > 0$ and $b_n(q)$ are positive real numbers. Under the condition that the terms $a_n (1-q/p^{lb_n(q)})$ form a sequence which satisfies the Karamata condition as $n\to\infty$, we establish complete convergence for $F(s)$ within the half-plane $\Re s > \sigma_0$, given that $\Im s \to\infty$.

This note offers a resolution to a metric version of a question posed by D. Gao, which was previously explored in a non-metric context in reference [6]. Specifically, if a metric group $G$ contains a subset $H$ such that any element in $G$ can be represented as the product of three terms: an element from $H$, an element from $G$'s complement, and another element from $H$, then a metric exists that only quantitatively preserves the distances within $H$.

We suggest a new computational method for estimating a log-concave probability density function, which is a common approach in nonparametric statistics. Our approach builds upon a non-parametric Bernstein-type approximation for the cumulative distribution function, utilizing a sequence of piecewise polynomial functions. We demonstrate that this method converges to the true density function at a rate of $O(1/n)$, and that the density estimates satisfy the log-concavity condition almost surely. Furthermore, our method allows for the efficient computation of maximum likelihood estimates and yields improved results in both synthetic and real-world data experiments compared to existing techniques.

The static configurations of granular systems can be analyzed using the volume ensemble, which involves generating various configurations of the same granular matter occupying a fixed volume. This approach is based on the granular configuration as the fundamental unit. The analysis of these configurations reveals that their inherent symmetries lead to an archetypal structure, making it challenging to determine unique microstates. This challenge is overcome by applying the Wang-Landau algorithm, an advanced Monte Carlo sampling method that efficiently explores the vast, arch-shaped microstate space. The algorithm is then used to calculate the microcanonical partition function, correcting for the arch-shaped microstate redundancy. The results of this approach are compared with the more traditional sampling method based on particle configuration, demonstrating the superiority of the new method in accurately capturing the microcanonical properties of granular systems.

We investigate a graph-based game, referred to as the Adventurer-Manager game, and its relationship to graph obstruction sets.  In this game, the Adventurer and the Manager are two players on a graph, with the Adventurer moving randomly while the Manager strategically placing obstacles in the Adventurer's path. The Adventurer wins if it reaches a designated destination before being trapped by the Manager's obstacles. An obstruction set for this game consists of all graphs from which the Adventurer cannot reach every other graph. Our research focuses on the Adventurer-Manager game, particularly on the minimal size of an obstruction set and the structure of the smallest obstruction sets.

The spectral distribution of a time series' frequency domain representation is a valuable indicator for understanding the statistical characteristics of the underlying time series. This statistical property not only provides insights into the time series itself, but also offers a useful tool for analyzing complex systems that are difficult to model directly. This work investigates the statistical properties of the spectral distribution of Gaussian processes, focusing on the relationships between different frequencies. Through analytical calculations, we find that the spectral distributions from different frequencies are interconnected, and the specific patterns of their interdependencies can reveal information about the system being analyzed.

This research paper explores the 1+1-dimensional Broer-Kaup system, a model derived from a two-dimensional integrable model, and its higher-order variant. The system, expressed through a pair of coupled ordinary differential equations, involves terms of order higher than one. The paper presents two types of 2D-1D systems, one with and another without mass term, and examines the solution's stability and long-term behavior. The study reveals that the system's long-term behavior is determined by a set of coupled ordinary differential equations, with the stability of a solution dependent on the initial conditions. The paper's main finding is that the system's long-term behavior is globally well-defined and dependent on the initial conditions. The study also reveals that the system's stability is dependent on the initial conditions and that the solution converges to a stable equilibrium point under certain conditions. The paper's results are presented in a table for easy reference.

This study focuses on the conservation of kinetic energy by weak solutions of the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations. Building on the concept of relative circulation introduced in \cite{IC} for tracking advected particles, we establish a new condition, utilizing the initial relative circulation and its relationship with the initial vorticity, to ensure the conservation of kinetic energy by weak solutions.

The VIRUP initiative offers an immersive experience, allowing users to step into a vast, 3D visualization of the cosmos. Through this platform, scientists can share their research with the general public, using interactive visualizations that bring the universe's complexity within reach of all. By making complex concepts more accessible, VIRUP's goal is to foster a deeper appreciation for astronomy and help users gain a deeper understanding of complex concepts through hands-on exploration.

The Data Bricks Cosmic Expedition is an interactive, data-based project designed to help kids understand the concept of data by mapping it to the physical world. Through this project, we aim to help kids make sense of data by transforming it into tangible objects, allowing them to visualize and interact with it. By utilizing a physical data visualization tool and incorporating a hands-on activity, we aim to help kids develop a deeper understanding of data. Our initial findings from a pilot study suggest that this project is effective in helping kids develop a concrete data representation, and we plan to further explore the potential of this project in educating kids about data.

A key feature of Software Defined Networking (SDN) is its ability to manage and control the flow of data packets through a network, making it more adaptable and efficient. This is achieved through the use of a logically centralized control plane that interacts with the data plane to facilitate packet forwarding. The data plane, typically implemented as a programmable hardware component, is designed to process and forward packets according to rules specified by the control plane. These rules are programmed into the data plane using a variety of programming languages and tools that enable the control of packet forwarding, classification, and other behaviors.

The increasing use of data-driven techniques in SDN has led to the development of new tools and languages that enable the expression of complex behaviors in data planes. This has made it possible to build sophisticated applications and services on top of SDN, such as network slicing and traffic engineering. However, the complexity of these new applications has also introduced new challenges, including the difficulty of identifying and understanding the functional data paths that are created by these complex behaviors. This paper proposes a novel approach to identifying and visualizing these functional data paths in SDN data planes, using a new metric called "flow similarity" to measure the similarity of individual flows and aggregate traffic patterns. The proposed approach is evaluated experimentally on a range of use cases and is shown to be effective in identifying interesting functional data paths in SDN data planes.

Our research introduces a novel approach to disentangled representation learning, which is achieved by integrating relational intelligence into generative adversarial networks (GANs). By developing a GAN framework that incorporates a relational capability, we are able to generate disentangled representations of multi-modal data. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in various applications, including data generation, classification, and image-to-image translation.

The concept of oscillating foil arrays has been successfully applied in various marine devices, such as wave and ocean power generators, rudders, and propellers, to improve performance and efficiency. However, the optimal design of these arrays remains a complex task, largely due to the intricate nature of wake interactions. To address this challenge, the current study focuses on the energy exchange between an oscillating foil and its trailing wake. The investigation involves a numerical model that simulates the wake using a two-dimensional, unsteady, incompressible Navier-Stokes solver, and the foil using a reduced-order model. The model is then used to analyze the energy engagement between the foil and wake, and the results are compared with experimental findings from a laboratory setup. The numerical model successfully replicates the energy engagement process, and the agreement between experimental and simulated results is satisfactory. The latter allows for the quantification of wake characteristics, such as velocity and vorticity, and the energy transfer between the foil and wake. The model is also capable of evaluating the energy collection efficiency of the foil array, and the results are compared with existing literature. The study's findings have significant implications for the design and optimization of oscillating foil arrays, and the proposed model can serve as a valuable tool for such endeavors.

We've developed a Bayesian method to estimate the real-time dynamics of physical observables in lattice QCD, starting from a basic principle. This method allows us to accurately calculate the real-time evolution of these observables, determine the uncertainty in our results, and test theoretical models. We've applied our approach to the real-time evolution of the proton's valence distribution function, simulating the impact of a high-energy photon. Our findings show that the initial distribution of partons has a significant impact on the outcome, and we can use this information to test theoretical models of parton distribution functions.

The interaction between a quantum dot and a superconductor is a crucial area of research, particularly when it comes to observing phenomena such as Josephson currents and charge-tunneling effects. By studying the interaction between a quantum dot and an Al island, scientists have been able to gain a deeper understanding of the behavior of these systems, including how the presence of an Andreev bound state can be detected through gate voltage measurements. By analyzing the data collected from the Al island using a superconducting gate, researchers were able to identify the mechanisms behind the charge-tunneling effects, including the influence of the superconducting proximity effect.

In the field of molecular generation, researchers have been striving to create models that can produce high-quality, innovative compounds with desirable properties. A significant advancement in this area has been the development of generative models that utilize energy-based methods. These new models effectively produce novel molecules that align with predefined goals, thanks to the inherent adversarial rejection of undesirable structures inherent in generative models. A notable example of this architecture is the Energy-based Molecular Generative Model, introduced by the DeepMind team, which utilizes pre-trained models to generate new molecules. Our study builds upon this architecture by introducing a novel energy-based generative model that leverages the Chemception neural network, a widely-used and well-established model in the field. Our experiments demonstrate that our model outperforms the EBM-VAE model, a different energy-based generative model, by producing target-oriented molecules with superior quality.

We introduce a novel mathematical model, the Dynamic Topology of Interaction Machine (DTIM), which encompasses a wide range of interactive models, including Petri Nets, Rewriting Systems, and Graph Transformation Systems, within a unified theoretical framework. Built on the concept of a token-directed graph, where tokens serve as the primary entities guiding graph transformations, the DTIM model facilitates a natural, step-by-step evolution through token movement and update rules, enabling the creation of a timeline that includes token positions and transitions at each step. This model also supports the concept of typed tokens, where each token is associated with a specific data type, and transitions can be triggered by the satisfaction of specific conditions linked to these tokens, enabling the implementation of complex, condition-driven interactions.

The Large Magellanic Cloud is surrounded by the Small Magellanic Cloud, with the latter's gravitational pull significantly affecting the former's structure. A recent study of the outer LMC's star members, using data from the VMC survey, has been conducted. By analyzing the proper motions of stars in the LMC's outer regions, the researchers were able to determine the movement of the LMC's stars and the impact of the SMC on its structure. A key finding of the research is that the stars in the outer regions of the LMC exhibit a significant difference in proper motion, with a value of 0.7 mas/yr, compared to the stars closer to the center. This difference is likely due to the influence of the SMC, with the researchers suggesting that the stars in the outer regions are shifted towards the SMC, while those closer to the center are shifted away from it. A further analysis of the research data has revealed that the stars in the outer regions of the LMC exhibit a higher velocity dispersion than those in the inner regions, with an average velocity of 100 km/s in the outer regions and 60 km/s in the inner regions. This is likely due to the influence of the SMC, with the researchers suggesting that the stars in the outer regions of the LMC exhibit a higher velocity dispersion than those in the inner regions. A comparison with previous research studies has revealed that the stars in the outer regions of the LMC exhibit a higher velocity

The growing concern of energy theft due to smart meter tampering necessitates the development of novel detection methods. This research presents a new approach, utilizing a deep learning framework to analyze smart meter data and mitigate the effects of tampering. A proposed system incorporates an advanced algorithm to detect energy theft, leveraging a combination of smart meter data and network configurations. The system's performance is evaluated through extensive simulations, comprising 1000 datasets, each consisting of 30 days' worth of data. The results demonstrate that the proposed system can detect energy theft with a high level of accuracy, yielding a mean average accuracy of 98.5% and a mean average precision of 98.5%, along with a recall of 98.5%.

We propose a general method, called induction, to generate tight surface networks 
that can be adapted to various types, such as simple trees, simple planar graphs, 
and specific graph types like the ones with a maximum degree of two. This method 
involves the construction of a tight surface network by gluing tight surface networks 
of a lower type. The induction process is demonstrated with the tree case and a 
one-vertex graph with five loops.

The lifetimes of the $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ and $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ baryons have been assessed using a sample of $443$ pb$^{-1}$ data from the LHCb experiment, which measured the ratio of branching fractions for $X^{0}$ decaying into $\Xi^{-}_c \pi^{+}$ and $\Omega^{-}_c \pi^{+}$, as well as the corresponding decay modes $X^{0} \rightarrow \Xi^{-}_c \pi^{+}$ and $\Omega^{-}_c \pi^{+}$. This allowed the determination of the lifetime ratio $\tau_{\Omega^{0}_{c}}/\tau_{\Xi^{0}_{c}}$ and individual baryon lifetimes. The results show that the $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ baryon lifetime is constrained between $100$ fs and $180 fs$, while the $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ lifetime is constrained between $170 fs$ and $195 fs$. These findings are in line with the current world averages and have been updated.

This paper introduces a novel, efficient, and accurate subspace clustering method for hyperspectral image classification, which incorporates both the inherent spectral properties and local spatial context of the data. The proposed approach, QuickSC, leverages a novel, highly effective similarity metric and a versatile spatio-spectral feature space that can be applied across different data types. By combining this similarity metric with a variety of spatial context techniques, including spatial filtering, spatial pyramid, and local auto-context, and a variety of spectral feature space techniques, including PCA, NMF, and independent component analysis, in both the spatial and spectral domains, the proposed approach effectively integrates diverse forms of data. The proposed approach, which is designed to be highly efficient and scalable, is capable of handling large datasets and can be parallelized. Experimental results on three hyperspectral images demonstrate the proposed approach's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

The Arctic's ice cover is primarily composed of a thick layer of old ice beneath a thinner layer of snow. The snow layer is constantly being replaced by new snowfall, but it also shifts due to wind. The snow's movement creates unique patterns, resembling snow dunes that form on the open, level ice. The formation process behind these patterns is influenced by the snow's compressibility and the way it responds to the weight of the ice beneath it. An idealized model, which simulates the behavior of a compressible snow layer, can accurately predict the formation of these patterns and their characteristics, such as their height, angle, and spacing. The model's predictions align with the observed patterns, but it has a limitation in not being able to account for the complex interactions between the snow and the underlying ice.

We explore the quantum Zeno effect in ultracold atom-molecule interactions within rapidly shifting magnetic fields. It's found that periodic changes in the magnetic field significantly reduce the rate of transition between atomic and molecular states due to the accumulation of dynamic phase. Moreover, we demonstrate that this phenomenon enables the creation of a robust molecular state by minimizing the probability of spin flip. The proposed research has significant potential for the development of novel methods to stabilize and manipulate ultracold atom-molecule mixtures.

A generalization of Itô's formula to nonextensive mechanics is presented, expanding on the classic differential equation with an additional parameter. This new formula extends the ito calculus to nonlinear Markov processes, which was previously addressed in a separate study. The extended Itô's formula is then applied to a financial model, representing the dynamics of a stock's price as a non-Markov process. The model is based on the idea that a stock's price is influenced by the previous prices, which is a common phenomenon in financial markets. The extended formula provides a way to capture this non-Markovian behavior, which is a common assumption in financial modeling. The model is also extended to include a broader class of financial models, which are often represented by stochastic differential equations.

A new class of nodal-line semimetal has been discovered, where the band structure is altered by light. This optically stimulated NLSS features a unique band structure in the dark state but exhibits a series of nodal points in the presence of light. The points are arranged in a complex pattern, with the introduction of a new type of topological feature, known as the nodal point with a Weyl point, characterized by a quadruplet structure. This topological feature is confirmed through its presence in the system's bulk energy spectrum and its surface state properties. Furthermore, an examination of the NLSS under specific conditions reveals the presence of nodal lines and their unique surface state properties.

The emergence of DCMs has led to the creation of a decentralized computing environment, enabling users to participate in the process and earn a reward for their contributions. However, existing DCMs are plagued by centralization issues, where a few dominant nodes can manipulate the system, leading to the concentration of computing power and control. In this context, we propose "Marvel DC," a new DCM that promotes decentralization, security, and fairness. By introducing a novel consensus mechanism and governance structure, Marvel DC ensures the distribution of computing power and rewards in a more equitable manner, fostering a more decentralized network. The protocol's architecture is designed to incentivize participation, prevent malicious behavior, and provide a robust, decentralized system, exemplified by its first implementation, E Marvel DC.

A new framework for assessing the visual quality of 3D point cloud references has been developed and applied to point cloud compression research. The framework utilizes a modified version of the VQEPQ model, which takes into consideration the reference image quality in addition to the compressed image quality. Through experiments, it was demonstrated that integrating reference quality into the evaluation process significantly enhances the model's accuracy. The framework's effectiveness was further validated by its ability to accurately predict the perceived quality of 3D point clouds when viewed through virtual reality head-mounted displays. The framework's practical application in rate-distortion point cloud compression was also explored.

We utilize holography to map the phase transition in finite-temperature QCD. The phase transition is identified in two distinct scenarios: non-saturation of the Borel-Cardona constraint, indicating a deconfinement transition, and a change in the number of infrared fixed points at high temperatures, marking the chiral transition. The study reveals that the deconfinement and chiral transitions coincide at low temperatures in weak coupling limits.

The self-supervised learning approach has achieved significant success in multiple domains, but its application to medical image analysis is still in its early stages. This research proposes a novel method, known as Slice-Based Self-Supervised Learning (SB-SSL), which is designed to improve the accuracy of anomaly classification in MRI scans of knees. The SB-SSL approach involves training a model to predict a slice's position in a 3D scan, and then using this prediction to create a new set of challenging labeled examples. The SB-SSL approach is based on a transformer network that can process multiple context slices simultaneously, and which is trained using a combination of easy and challenging labeled examples.
